content:
**The five most‑planted grape varieties in Bordeaux (by vineyard area) and the part of the region where they are most heavily grown**

| Rank | Grape Variety | Approx. % of Bordeaux vineyards | Area(s) where it is most planted | Notes |
|------|---------------|---------------------------------|----------------------------------|-------|
| 1 | **Merlot** | ~ 50 % | **Right Bank** – Saint‑Émilion, Pomerol, Graves (both red‑and‑white). | Merlot is the backbone of the Right‑Bank blends and the dominant grape in the prestigious Saint‑Émilion and Pomerol appellations. |
| 2 | **Cabernet Sauvignon** | ~ 25–30 % | **Left Bank** – Médoc (Pauillac, Margaux, Saint‑Julien, etc.), Graves (red). | Cabernet Sauvignon gives structure, tannin and age‑potential to the classic Left‑Bank blends. |
| 3 | **Cabernet Franc** | ~ 15 % | **Right Bank** (Saint‑Émilion, Pomerol, Graves) – also some plantings on the Left Bank where it provides aromatics and freshness. | Often a “bridge” grape, it adds spice and floral notes to Bordeaux blends. |
| 4 | **Petit Verdot** | ~ 2 % | **Left Bank** – mainly used in the Médoc and Graves as a blending grape; plantings are concentrated in the more traditional, tannic blends. | Rare on its own, but essential for adding color and subtle tannin to the classic Bordeaux blend. |
| 5 | **Malbec** | ~ 1 % | **Graves (Right Bank)** – mostly in the red‑Grapes of Graves, sometimes in the white Graves as a minor component. | Once a major variety, Malbec is now a niche player, prized for its deep colour and softness. |

---

### Quick‑refer guide

| Grape | Most‑planted area | Typical role |
|-------|-------------------|--------------|
| Merlot | Right Bank (Saint‑Émilion, Pomerol, Graves) | Main fruit in the right‑bank blends; often the sole grape in Pomerol. |
| Cabernet Sauvignon | Left Bank (Médoc, Graves) | Provides structure, tannin, and age‑potential. |
| Cabernet Franc | Right Bank (Saint‑Émilion, Pomerol, Graves) | Adds aromatics, spice, and a lighter body. |
| Petit Verdot | Left Bank (Médoc, Graves) | Minor blending grape for color and subtle tannin. |
| Malbec | Graves (Right Bank) | Minor blending grape; occasionally used for single‑varietal reds. |

> **Why this matters**  
> Understanding where each grape dominates helps you anticipate the style and structure of a bottle. For example, a red from **Saint‑Émilion** will almost always be very Merlot‑heavy, while a **Pauillac** wine will be more Cabernet Sauvignon‑centric with a touch of Cabernet Franc.  

Feel free to ask if you’d like more details on any specific appellation or blending practice!
